category: User Language: builtin functions (network, strings, time, objects, XML)
description: ULP builtin functions, part 2: network requests (netget, netpost, neterror), formatted printing (printf, sprintf), string functions (strchr ... strxstr), URN functions for managed-library objects, time functions and conversions, object functions for groups and assembly variants (clrgroup, ingroup, setgroup, setvariant, variant) and XML parsing functions. Source: EAGLE 9.6.0 built-in help.

tools.name: neterror
tools.description: Returns a text describing the error of the most recent network function call, or an empty string if it succeeded. Call it after netget() or netpost() returned a negative value and show the message to the user.
tools.notes: For HTTPS failures the message usually points to missing or expired certificates on the system.

tools.name: netget
tools.description: Sends an HTTP, HTTPS or FTP GET request and stores the response in the destination variable, returning the number of objects read or a negative value on error. As with fileread(), the destination type selects binary (char array), line-wise text (string array) or whole-text (string) mode. The connection is dropped after the optional timeout in seconds without network activity (default 20).
tools.usage: int netget(dest, string url[, int timeout]);   // dest: char[] | string[] | string

parameters.name: dest
parameters.description: char array, string array or string receiving the response.

parameters.name: url
parameters.description: Full URL with protocol (http, https or ftp).

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Seconds without activity before the connection is terminated (default 20).

tools.notes: The url must include the protocol and may carry name=value parameters or userid:password@ credentials (avoid putting secrets into ULPs). A string destination is truncated at the first 0x00 byte, so use a char array for binary data. Proxies are configured in the Control Panel under Help/Check for Update/Configure. Network access sends data off the machine; only use it where that is allowed.

tools.name: netpost
tools.description: Sends data with an HTTP or HTTPS POST request and stores the response in the destination variable, returning the number of objects read or a negative value on error. The default content type is "text/html; charset=utf-8" and can be overridden; timeout and destination types work as in netget().
tools.usage: int netpost(dest, string url, string data[, int timeout[, string content_type]]);

parameters.name: dest
parameters.description: char array, string array or string receiving the response.

tools.notes: Only HTTP and HTTPS are supported for POST. The same SSL and proxy notes as for netget() apply.

tools.name: printf
tools.description: Writes formatted text to the file opened by the most recent (innermost active) output() statement and returns the number of characters written, or -1 on error. The format string contains plain characters and % conversion specifications; argument count and types are checked against the format, and mismatches are reported as errors. Unlike sprintf(), printf can write binary zero characters.
tools.usage:
int printf(string format[, argument, ...]);
format spec: %[flags][width][.prec]type
  type:  d o u x X (int)  f e E g G (real)  c (char)  s (string)  %% (percent sign)
  flags: -  left-justify   +  always sign   ' ' blank before positive values
  width: n  (pad with blanks)   0n (pad with zeros)   *  (taken from an int argument)
  .prec: .n  decimals for e/E/f, significant digits for g/G, max. characters for s, min. digits for d/o/u/x/X

parameters.name: format
parameters.description: Format string with plain text and % specifications.

parameters.name: argument
parameters.description: Values matching the specifications in number and type.

tools.notes: Use printf inside an output() block (or a function called from one). Default precision is 6 for e/E/f; .0 suppresses the decimal point for reals. Width never truncates a value. Coordinates must be converted with u2mm() etc. before printing with %f.

tools.name: sprintf
tools.description: Formats values into a string variable using the same format specifications as printf() and returns the number of characters written, or -1 on error. It is the way to turn numbers into text for dialogs, command strings for exit() and file names.
tools.usage: int sprintf(string result, string format[, argument, ...]);

parameters.name: result
parameters.description: String variable that receives the formatted text.

tools.notes: The result cannot contain binary zero characters: everything after a 0x00 is dropped (use printf for binary output). result is overwritten, not appended - use a temporary string and += to build longer texts.

tools.name: strchr
tools.description: Returns the position of the first occurrence of a character in a string, or -1 if it does not occur. An optional start index begins the search at that position; negative values count from the end of the string.
tools.usage: int strchr(string s, char c[, int index]);

parameters.name: index
parameters.description: Optional start position; negative counts from the end.

tools.notes: See strrchr() for the last occurrence and strstr() for substrings.

tools.name: strjoin
tools.description: Joins all elements of a string array into one string, separated by the given character. With '\n' as separator the result also ends with a newline, which makes it the inverse of reading a text file with fileread() and splitting it with strsplit().
tools.notes: The separator is a single char, not a string. See strsplit() for the reverse operation.

tools.name: strlen
tools.description: Returns the number of characters in a string. Use it for loops over characters, padding and truncation.
tools.notes: s[strlen(s)] is always 0, so for (i = 0; s[i]; ++i) iterates without calling strlen.

tools.name: strlwr
tools.description: Returns a copy of the string with all upper-case letters converted to lower case; the argument itself is not changed. Use it for case-insensitive comparisons and normalized file names.
tools.example:
string f = "D:/Work/BOARD.BRD";
if (strlwr(fileext(f)) == ".brd") dlgMessageBox("board file");
tools.notes: See strupr() and tolower().

tools.name: strrchr
tools.description: Returns the position of the last occurrence of a character in a string, or -1. An optional index sets where the search starts, negative values counting from the end. It is useful for splitting at the last separator, e.g. directory or suffix delimiters.
tools.usage: int strrchr(string s, char c[, int index]);
tools.notes: See strchr() and strrstr().

tools.name: strrstr
tools.description: Returns the position of the last occurrence of a substring in a string, or -1. An optional index sets the start position (negative from the end).
tools.usage: int strrstr(string s1, string s2[, int index]);
tools.example:
string Path = "a/b/c/lib/lib/x.lbr";
int p = strrstr(Path, "/lib/");          // 9 (start of the last /lib/)
tools.notes: See strstr() for the first occurrence.

tools.name: strsplit
tools.description: Splits a string at a separator character into the elements of a string array and returns the number of fields. With '\n' as separator a trailing empty field is dropped, so splitting a text file's content gives one element per line; with other separators a trailing empty field counts ("a:b:c:" gives 4 fields).
tools.usage: int strsplit(string &array[], string s, char separator);
tools.notes: The separator is a single char; quoted fields are not recognized (use lookup() for quoted CSV-like records).

tools.name: strstr
tools.description: Returns the position of the first occurrence of a substring in a string, or -1 if it does not occur. An optional index sets the start position (negative counts from the end). Comparing the result with 0 is a simple starts-with test.
tools.usage: int strstr(string s1, string s2[, int index]);
tools.notes: Case-sensitive; combine with strupr() for case-insensitive search. strxstr() searches with regular expressions.

tools.name: strsub
tools.description: Returns the substring starting at a position with an optional length; without length the rest of the string is returned. An empty string results if start lies outside the string or the length is not positive.
tools.usage: string strsub(string s, int start[, int length]);
tools.notes: Positions are 0-based.

tools.name: strtod
tools.description: Converts the leading part of a string to a real number, stopping at the first character that does not fit a real constant; returns 0.0 if nothing can be converted. Use it to parse numbers from dialogs, attributes or data files.

parameters.name: s
parameters.description: String starting with a real number.

tools.notes: Returns 0.0 on errors, which cannot be distinguished from a real 0 - validate input if that matters. Unit suffixes such as 'k' or 'u' in part values are not interpreted.

tools.name: strtol
tools.description: Converts the leading part of a string to an int, stopping at the first character that does not fit an integer constant; returns 0 if nothing can be converted. Leading 0 and 0x select octal and hexadecimal as for integer constants.
tools.notes: Because a leading zero means octal, "010" converts to 8 - strip leading zeros from numeric text first.

tools.name: strupr
tools.description: Returns a copy of the string with all lower-case letters converted to upper case; the argument is not changed. Typical use is case-insensitive matching of names and options.
tools.example:
if (argc > 1 && strupr(argv[1]) == "/HELP") { dlgMessageBox(usage); exit(0); }
board(B) B.signals(S) if (strupr(S.name) == "GND") { /* ... */ }
tools.notes: See strlwr() and toupper().

tools.name: strxstr
tools.description: Searches a string for the first match of a regular expression and returns its position, or -1. An optional start index works as for strstr(), and an optional int variable receives the length of the matched text.
tools.usage: int strxstr(string s1, string s2[, int index[, int &length]]);

parameters.name: index
parameters.description: Start position (negative counts from the end).

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Receives the length of the matching substring.

tools.notes: s2 is a regular expression: '.' any character, '*' repetition etc. (e.g. "i.*a" matches "is a"). Escape regex special characters when searching literally.

tools.name: urnbase
tools.description: Returns the base part of a URN without the trailing /version, e.g. urn:adsk.eagle:footprint:123 for urn:adsk.eagle:footprint:123/4. URNs identify managed-library objects (device sets, footprints, symbols, 3D packages); if no version is present the input is returned unchanged.
tools.example:
board(B) output("3d-urns.txt", "wt") B.elements(E)
  if (E.package3d) printf("%s %s v%d\n", E.name, urnbase(E.package3d.urn), urnversion(E.package3d.urn));
tools.notes: See urnversion().

tools.name: urnversion
tools.description: Returns the version number that follows the '/' of a URN, or -1 if the URN has no version. Use it to compare the library object versions used in a design.
tools.example:
string urn = "urn:adsk.eagle:footprint:123/4";
int v = urnversion(urn);               // 4
tools.notes: See urnbase().

tools.name: time
tools.description: Returns the current system time as seconds since a system-dependent reference date. The value can be broken down or formatted with the t2... functions and compared with filetime().
tools.example:
int Now = time();
output("log.txt", "at") printf("%s  run by %s\n", t2string(Now, "yyyy-MM-dd hh:mm:ss"), argv[0]);
tools.notes: Resolution is one second; for measuring durations use timems(). time is a builtin name and cannot be used for a variable.

tools.name: timems
tools.description: Returns the number of milliseconds elapsed since the ULP was started. Use it to measure how long parts of a program take; the counter wraps to 0 every 24 hours.
tools.notes: Wraps around after 86400000 ms.

tools.name: t2day, t2dayofweek, t2hour, t2minute, t2month, t2second, t2year
tools.description: Break a time value (from time() or filetime()) into its parts in local time: day of month 1..31, day of week 0 (Sunday)..6, hour 0..23, minute 0..59, month 0..11, second 0..59 and the four-digit year.
tools.usage:
int t2day(int t);   int t2dayofweek(int t);   int t2hour(int t);   int t2minute(int t);
int t2month(int t); int t2second(int t);      int t2year(int t);
tools.notes: t2month is 0-based (0 = January): add 1 for display. For formatted strings t2string() with a format is simpler.

tools.name: t2string
tools.description: Converts a time value into a formatted date/time string. Without a format a country-specific local time string is produced; with a format string, expressions such as yyyy, MM, dd, hh, mm, ss, ddd/MMM names and AP are replaced, and a leading U produces UTC.

parameters.name: t
parameters.description: Time value from time() or filetime().

parameters.name: format
parameters.description: Optional format string; omitted = localized default.

tools.notes: Characters that are not format expressions are copied as-is; quote literal text containing letters like d, M, h, m, s in single quotes. z/zzz are always 0 because the time has one-second resolution.

tools.name: clrgroup
tools.description: Clears the group flags of an object so it is no longer part of the group defined in the editor. Applied to a container such as UL_BOARD or UL_NET it clears the flags of all contained objects recursively.
tools.notes: The same limitations as for setgroup() apply to recursive clearing (not UL_LIBRARY/UL_SCHEMATIC, not non-selectable sub-objects).

tools.name: ingroup
tools.description: Tells whether an object belongs to the group currently defined in the editor, so a ULP can process only the user's selection. When a ULP is started from a context menu, the clicked object forms a one-element group and ingroup() identifies it. For wires the result tells which end points are in the group.
tools.notes: Point objects (texts, vias, circles...) are in the group if their coordinate is. UL_WIRE returns 0-3 (bit 0 = first, bit 1 = second end point). UL_RECTANGLE/UL_FRAME return corner bits (0 upper right, 1 upper left, 2 lower left, 3 lower right). Containers (UL_NET, UL_SEGMENT, UL_SIGNAL, UL_POLYGON, UL_SHEET, UL_DEVICESET, UL_SYMBOL, UL_FOOTPRINT) are non-zero if any contained object is; UL_CONTACTREF/UL_PINREF follow the referenced contact/pin. For UL_GRID, UL_VARIANT and text/frame wires the result is undefined.

tools.name: setgroup
tools.description: Adds an object to the editor's group, as a whole or only selected points (for a wire: 1 = first, 2 = second, 3 = both end points). Applied to a container like UL_BOARD or UL_NET, all selectable contained objects are added recursively. After the ULP ends the group can be used by commands such as MOVE, CHANGE or DELETE with the group mouse click.

parameters.name: flags
parameters.description: Optional point mask; for UL_WIRE 1 = first, 2 = second, 3 = both end points.

tools.notes: Previously set group flags stay set. Not recursive for UL_LIBRARY and UL_SCHEMATIC; non-selectable parts (UL_GRID, UL_VARIANT, wires of texts/frames) are not flagged.

tools.name: setvariant
tools.description: Makes the named assembly variant current for the rest of the ULP, so that populate flags, values and technologies of parts are seen as defined in that variant. Returns non-zero if the variant exists. The drawing's own variant is restored when the ULP ends.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Name of an assembly variant defined in the current drawing.

tools.notes: In a board, setting a variant only works if the consistent schematic is loaded. Loop over variantdefs() to process all variants; save variant() first to know the original one.

tools.name: variant
tools.description: Returns the name of the current assembly variant, or an empty string if none is selected. Use it to label outputs or to restore the variant after switching with setvariant().
tools.notes: variant is a builtin name and cannot be used for a variable. The shipped save-brd-variants.ulp additionally treats the literal string '' as the default variant, so test for both when naming files.

tools.name: xmlattribute
tools.description: Returns the value of one attribute of a tag within XML text. The tag is given as a path such as "eagle/drawing/board"; if the attribute occurs more than once in the tag, the last value is used. Together with fileread() it lets a ULP read XML files, including EAGLE's own .brd/.sch/.lbr files.
tools.usage: string xmlattribute(string xml, string tag, string attribute);
tools.notes: Malformed XML makes every XML function return an empty result and shows a warning with the line/column inside the given string. The path refers to the first matching element; use xmlelements() to visit repeated tags.

tools.name: xmlattributes
tools.description: Stores the names of all attributes of a tag in a string array and returns their number. The order does not necessarily follow the XML text, and each name appears once even if repeated.
tools.usage: int xmlattributes(string &array[], string xml, string tag);
tools.notes: The tag is a path; see xmlattribute() for reading values.

tools.name: xmlelement
tools.description: Returns the complete first element with the given tag path, including its outer tags, so it can be processed further with the other XML functions. Plain-text whitespace is kept, although tag formatting and attribute order may differ from the original.
tools.notes: Only the first occurrence is returned; use xmlelements() for all of them. Paths inside the returned element start at its own tag.

tools.name: xmlelements
tools.description: Like xmlelement(), but stores every element matching the tag path in a string array and returns how many were found. It is the way to iterate over repeated XML elements such as the parts, signals or settings of a file.
tools.usage: int xmlelements(string &array[], string xml, string tag);
tools.notes: Each array element contains the element with its outer tag, so subsequent paths start with that tag name.

tools.name: xmltags
tools.description: Stores the distinct tag names found directly below the given tag path in a string array and returns their number. With an empty path it returns the root tag name. Use it to explore unknown XML structures.
tools.usage: int xmltags(string &array[], string xml, string tag);
tools.notes: Each tag name is reported once, even if it occurs several times.

tools.name: xmltext
tools.description: Returns the text content of an element with all inner tags stripped; whitespace including newlines is kept. Use it for elements such as descriptions whose content is text.
tools.notes: Returns the text of the first matching element; combine with xmlelements() for repeated ones.
